serviceSummary: Prescription Dispensing covers NHS and private medicines supply with pharmacist clinical screening, accuracy checking and patient counselling at every handover. Community pharmacies validate prescriptions, identify interactions, prepare labelled medicines and explain safe use — supporting adherence and reducing medicines-related harm.

mythsVsFacts.myth: Dispensing is just labelling a box.
mythsVsFacts.fact: Dispensing includes clinical validation, preparation, accuracy checking and patient counselling.

mythsVsFacts.myth: Any shop can dispense prescriptions.
mythsVsFacts.fact: Only GPhC-registered pharmacies with a superintendent pharmacist may dispense prescriptions.

mythsVsFacts.myth: Pharmacists never contact the GP.
mythsVsFacts.fact: Pharmacists query prescribers when clinical concerns arise before supply.

mythsVsFacts.myth: EPS means instant supply always.
mythsVsFacts.fact: Clinical checks and stock availability still affect supply timing.

mythsVsFacts.myth: You do not need counselling on repeats.
mythsVsFacts.fact: Counselling is offered when medicines change or patients have questions.

mythsVsFacts.myth: Private and NHS dispensing skip clinical checks.
mythsVsFacts.fact: The same clinical governance applies to all prescription supply.

mythsVsFacts.myth: Pharmacists diagnose conditions at dispensing.
mythsVsFacts.fact: Pharmacists screen for safety — diagnosis remains with the prescriber.

mythsVsFacts.myth: It is safe to share dispensed medicines.
mythsVsFacts.fact: Medicines are prescribed for individuals — sharing is unsafe and illegal.

mythsVsFacts.myth: Delivery skips counselling.
mythsVsFacts.fact: Counselling may be provided by phone or with delivery documentation.

mythsVsFacts.myth: All prescriptions are ready in minutes.
mythsVsFacts.fact: New prescriptions need clinical checks — timing varies.

mythsVsFacts.myth: Prescription Dispensing replaces all GP care.
mythsVsFacts.fact: Prescription Dispensing complements GP services — chronic and complex conditions remain with your GP.

mythsVsFacts.myth: Every patient automatically qualifies for Prescription Dispensing.
mythsVsFacts.fact: Individual clinical assessment confirms suitability for prescription dispensing.

mythsVsFacts.myth: Prescription Dispensing is always free.
mythsVsFacts.fact: NHS eligibility and commissioning determine cost — private prescription dispensing may incur disclosed fees.

mythsVsFacts.myth: Walk-in guarantees immediate Prescription Dispensing.
mythsVsFacts.fact: Booking may be required; clinical assessment always precedes supply.

mythsVsFacts.myth: Online research removes the need for Prescription Dispensing.
mythsVsFacts.fact: Personalised assessment and supply decisions require a pharmacist consultation.

mythsVsFacts.myth: Prescription Dispensing treats emergencies.
mythsVsFacts.fact: Emergencies need 999 or A&E — prescription dispensing is not an emergency service.

mythsVsFacts.myth: Side effects from Prescription Dispensing should be ignored.
mythsVsFacts.fact: Report side effects promptly to the pharmacy or GP.

mythsVsFacts.myth: All pharmacies offer identical Prescription Dispensing.
mythsVsFacts.fact: Commissioning, training and private service menus vary locally.

mythsVsFacts.myth: No follow-up is needed after Prescription Dispensing.
mythsVsFacts.fact: Safety-netting and review are essential parts of safe care.

mythsVsFacts.myth: Prescription Dispensing always includes medicine supply.
mythsVsFacts.fact: Advice-only outcomes are valid when supply is not clinically appropriate.

mythsVsFacts.myth: Pharmacists are not qualified for Prescription Dispensing.
mythsVsFacts.fact: GPhC-registered pharmacists deliver prescription dispensing under clinical governance.

mythsVsFacts.myth: Prescription Dispensing is the same as a GP appointment.
mythsVsFacts.fact: Prescription Dispensing operates within defined pharmacy scope with referral when needed.

mythsVsFacts.myth: Sharing Prescription Dispensing medicines is acceptable.
mythsVsFacts.fact: Prescription medicines are individualised — never share.

mythsVsFacts.myth: Prescription Dispensing needs no preparation.
mythsVsFacts.fact: Some appointments require specific preparation — confirm at booking.

mythsVsFacts.myth: NHS and private Prescription Dispensing are identical.
mythsVsFacts.fact: NHS pathways have eligibility criteria; private scope may differ.

faqLibrary.question: How long does prescription dispensing take?
faqLibrary.answer: New prescriptions typically need 24–48 hours for clinical checks; repeats may be faster once your record is established.

faqLibrary.question: What is EPS nomination?
faqLibrary.answer: Electronic Prescription Service sends prescriptions from your GP to a nominated pharmacy digitally. The pharmacy team provides evidence-based guidance tailored to your situation, with clear safety-netting before you leave.

faqLibrary.question: Can someone collect my prescription for me?
faqLibrary.answer: Yes — carers and proxies may collect with appropriate identification, especially for controlled drugs. The pharmacy team provides evidence-based guidance tailored to your situation, with clear safety-netting before you leave.

faqLibrary.question: What if my medicine is out of stock?
faqLibrary.answer: The pharmacy orders stock or advises on partial supply and expected timing. The pharmacy team provides evidence-based guidance tailored to your situation, with clear safety-netting before you leave.

faqLibrary.question: Do I need ID to collect controlled drugs?
faqLibrary.answer: Photo identification is typically required for Schedule 2 and 3 controlled medicines. The pharmacy team provides evidence-based guidance tailored to your situation, with clear safety-netting before you leave.

faqLibrary.question: Will the pharmacist explain my new medicine?
faqLibrary.answer: Yes — counselling on new or changed medicines is part of safe dispensing. The pharmacy team provides evidence-based guidance tailored to your situation, with clear safety-netting before you leave.

faqLibrary.question: Can I use any pharmacy for my prescription?
faqLibrary.answer: You may use any pharmacy, but EPS nomination sends prescriptions to your chosen pharmacy electronically. The pharmacy team provides evidence-based guidance tailored to your situation, with clear safety-netting before you leave.

faqLibrary.question: What happens if the pharmacist finds a problem?
faqLibrary.answer: They contact the prescriber to resolve queries before supply. The pharmacy team provides evidence-based guidance tailored to your situation, with clear safety-netting before you leave.

faqLibrary.question: Are generic medicines as effective as branded?
faqLibrary.answer: Generic medicines contain the same active ingredient and meet the same quality standards. The pharmacy team provides evidence-based guidance tailored to your situation, with clear safety-netting before you leave.

faqLibrary.question: Can I get a prescription delivered?
faqLibrary.answer: Many pharmacies offer delivery — ask the team about eligibility and charges. The pharmacy team provides evidence-based guidance tailored to your situation, with clear safety-netting before you leave.

faqLibrary.question: Do I need an appointment for Prescription Dispensing?
faqLibrary.answer: Booking ahead for Prescription Dispensing ensures adequate consultation time. Walk-in availability varies by pharmacy and season — call to confirm same-day capacity.

faqLibrary.question: Is Prescription Dispensing free on the NHS?
faqLibrary.answer: NHS-funded Prescription Dispensing is free where the service is commissioned and you meet eligibility criteria. Private prescription dispensing may incur a disclosed fee confirmed before supply.

faqLibrary.question: How long does a Prescription Dispensing appointment take?
faqLibrary.answer: Prescription Dispensing consultations typically take 15–45 minutes depending on assessment complexity, counselling depth and whether tests or supply are involved.

faqLibrary.question: Who is eligible for Prescription Dispensing?
faqLibrary.answer: Eligibility for Prescription Dispensing depends on clinical criteria, age, medical history and local NHS commissioning. Suitability is confirmed individually — not assumed at booking.

faqLibrary.question: What should I bring to my Prescription Dispensing appointment?
faqLibrary.answer: Bring a complete medicines list, allergy history, relevant test results, travel itinerary if applicable, and photo ID for NHS or controlled services.

faqLibrary.question: Can I speak to a pharmacist before booking Prescription Dispensing?
faqLibrary.answer: Yes — a brief phone triage helps confirm whether Prescription Dispensing is appropriate, explains fees or NHS eligibility, and sets preparation expectations.

faqLibrary.question: What if I am not eligible for Prescription Dispensing?
faqLibrary.answer: If Prescription Dispensing is not suitable, the pharmacist signposts you to GP, NHS 111, sexual health services or urgent care with documented advice.

faqLibrary.question: How much does private Prescription Dispensing cost?
faqLibrary.answer: Private prescription dispensing fees vary by pharmacy and service complexity. Costs are explained before supply — ask for a clear quote at booking.

faqLibrary.question: What happens during a Prescription Dispensing consultation?
faqLibrary.answer: The pharmacist reviews history, confirms consent, assesses suitability, explains options with risks and benefits, and documents agreed next steps.

faqLibrary.question: When should I see a GP instead of Prescription Dispensing?
faqLibrary.answer: Persistent, severe or worsening symptoms, pregnancy complications, systemic illness and emergency presentations need GP or urgent care — not prescription dispensing alone.

faqLibrary.question: Can I use Prescription Dispensing for my child?
faqLibrary.answer: Paediatric prescription dispensing depends on age limits per pathway. Contact the pharmacy to confirm guardian requirements and commissioned paediatric scope.

faqLibrary.question: Is Prescription Dispensing confidential?
faqLibrary.answer: Yes — Prescription Dispensing takes place in a private consultation room. Records are held under pharmacy confidentiality and GDPR standards.

faqLibrary.question: What follow-up is needed after Prescription Dispensing?
faqLibrary.answer: Follow safety-netting advice, attend booked reviews, and contact the pharmacy or GP if symptoms persist, side effects occur or concerns arise.

faqLibrary.question: Does Prescription Dispensing require a GP referral?
faqLibrary.answer: Many pharmacy services including prescription dispensing are self-referral — referral requirements depend on the specific pathway and local commissioning.

faqLibrary.question: How do I book Prescription Dispensing at the pharmacy?
faqLibrary.answer: Book online, by phone or in person. The team confirms availability, eligibility, fees and preparation instructions for Prescription Dispensing.

faqLibrary.question: What are the risks of Prescription Dispensing?
faqLibrary.answer: Risks depend on the individual and any supplied treatment. The pharmacist explains side effects, contraindications and when to seek urgent help.

faqLibrary.question: Can I get Prescription Dispensing on the same day?
faqLibrary.answer: Same-day prescription dispensing may be available for urgent or seasonal services — contact the pharmacy early as appointments fill quickly.

faqLibrary.question: Will my GP be informed after Prescription Dispensing?
faqLibrary.answer: Where clinically appropriate, consultation outcomes may be shared with your GP to support continuity — this is explained before proceeding.

faqLibrary.question: What qualifications deliver Prescription Dispensing?
faqLibrary.answer: Prescription Dispensing is delivered by GPhC-registered pharmacists and trained staff under clinical governance, PGDs or protocols where commissioned.

faqLibrary.question: Can I cancel or reschedule Prescription Dispensing?
faqLibrary.answer: Yes — contact the pharmacy promptly to reschedule. For time-sensitive services such as emergency contraception, rebook as soon as possible.

faqLibrary.question: Is Prescription Dispensing better than going to my GP?
faqLibrary.answer: Prescription Dispensing complements GP care for suitable presentations — it does not replace GP diagnosis or long-term condition management.

faqLibrary.question: What is the difference between NHS and private Prescription Dispensing?
faqLibrary.answer: NHS prescription dispensing follows commissioned eligibility and may be free; private services offer broader access with disclosed fees and may include options outside NHS scope.

faqLibrary.question: Why choose a pharmacy for Prescription Dispensing instead of a clinic?
faqLibrary.answer: Community pharmacies offer convenient access, extended hours and integrated medicines expertise — suitable for many patients without hospital referral.

faqLibrary.question: Can I claim Prescription Dispensing on private medical insurance?
faqLibrary.answer: Insurance coverage for prescription dispensing varies by policy. The pharmacy provides receipts; check with your insurer before booking.

faqLibrary.question: What if I cannot afford private Prescription Dispensing?
faqLibrary.answer: Ask about NHS eligibility or signposting to NHS pathways. The pharmacy team explains free options and alternative services where available.

faqLibrary.question: Is Prescription Dispensing safe if I take other medicines?
faqLibrary.answer: Bring your full medicines list — the pharmacist checks interactions and contraindications before any supply related to Prescription Dispensing.

faqLibrary.question: What should I do if Prescription Dispensing does not work?
faqLibrary.answer: Return for review or see your GP if symptoms persist beyond the expected recovery window explained at your prescription dispensing consultation.

faqLibrary.question: Can I get Prescription Dispensing without registering with a GP?
faqLibrary.answer: Some prescription dispensing services do not require GP registration, but ongoing care usually benefits from GP linkage — confirm locally.

faqLibrary.question: Does Prescription Dispensing include a written summary?
faqLibrary.answer: Many consultations include written advice or supply labels. Ask for a summary for your records or employer if needed. The pharmacy team provides evidence-based guidance tailored to your situation, with clear safety-netting before you leave.

faqLibrary.question: Are evening or weekend Prescription Dispensing appointments available?
faqLibrary.answer: Extended hours vary by pharmacy — contact the team for weekend and evening prescription dispensing availability in your area.

faqLibrary.question: How do I prepare questions for Prescription Dispensing?
faqLibrary.answer: Write down symptoms, duration, medicines tried and concerns about cost or eligibility — this helps the pharmacist tailor prescription dispensing advice.

faqLibrary.question: What red flags mean I should not use Prescription Dispensing?
faqLibrary.answer: Chest pain, breathing difficulty, severe bleeding, confusion, stroke symptoms and pregnancy emergencies need urgent care — not routine prescription dispensing.

faqLibrary.question: Can carers book Prescription Dispensing for someone else?
faqLibrary.answer: Carers may book on behalf of others with appropriate consent and identification — especially for housebound or vulnerable patients.

faqLibrary.question: Is Prescription Dispensing suitable if I am pregnant or breastfeeding?
faqLibrary.answer: Pregnancy and breastfeeding affect eligibility for many medicines and services — declare this at assessment for safe prescription dispensing advice.

faqLibrary.question: How often can I repeat Prescription Dispensing?
faqLibrary.answer: Repeat access depends on clinical need and pathway rules — the pharmacist explains appropriate intervals for prescription dispensing.

faqLibrary.question: What evidence supports Prescription Dispensing at pharmacies?
faqLibrary.answer: Prescription Dispensing follows NHS specifications, NICE guidance where applicable, and GPhC professional standards for safe pharmacy-led care.

faqLibrary.question: Will Prescription Dispensing delay me seeing a specialist?
faqLibrary.answer: Appropriate pharmacy care can resolve suitable cases quickly; referral to GP or specialist occurs when prescription dispensing falls outside scope.

faqLibrary.question: Can I use Prescription Dispensing while travelling?
faqLibrary.answer: For travel-related services, bring itinerary dates and previous vaccination records. Non-travel prescription dispensing is usually locality-based — confirm access.

faqLibrary.question: What languages or accessibility support is available for Prescription Dispensing?
faqLibrary.answer: Pharmacies provide reasonable adjustments under equality duties — ask about access needs when booking prescription dispensing.

faqLibrary.question: Does Prescription Dispensing include blood tests or screening?
faqLibrary.answer: Some prescription dispensing pathways include point-of-care tests where equipment is available — confirm what is included when booking.
